RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving
Meta-Agent 
Huan Zhang 1, † , Mingju Chen 1, † , Dongxu Zhou 1 , Can Lv 1 , Sen Cui 2 ,
Faguo Wu 1,* ,   Shiji Zhou 1,2,3,* 
1 Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Future Blockchain and Privacy Computing, School of Artificial Intelligence,
Beihang University,   2 Tsinghua University,   3 Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI), 
† Equal contribution.   Corresponding to:   Shiji Zhou <zhoushiji25@buaa.edu.cn> 
Abstract 
Large language model (LLM) agents have
demonstrated strong capabilities in complex
tasks, including code generation, tool use, and
multi-hop question answering. Existing self-
improvement methods enhance agent perfor-
mance through model optimization, harness
evolution, and executable artifact refinement,
while recursive self-improvement (RSI) fur-
ther extends optimization to the improvement
mechanisms themselves. However, adapting
self-improvement workflows to evolving per-
formance bottlenecks while improving work-
flow orchestration through execution feedback
remains a key challenge. We propose   RSIFlow ,
a   R ecursive   S elf- I mprovement framework that
integrates adaptive work flow   orchestration with
meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow di-
agnoses performance bottlenecks from task-
agent trajectories and environmental feedback
to dynamically select component-specific im-
provement workflows.   The meta-agent then
distills workflow outcomes into component-
specific skills and cross-component principles,
evolving its own harness to improve subse-
quent workflow orchestration.   Experiments
across six benchmarks and two backbone mod-
els show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA av-
erage performance on all benchmarks. Abla-
tion studies further demonstrate the contribu-
tions of adaptive workflow orchestration and
meta-harness evolution. Code is available at
https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow. 
1   Introduction 
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in
coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answer-
ing (Yang et al., 2024; Schick et al., 2023; Yao
et al., 2023). To continuously enhance the devel-
opment of agents’ capabilities in task domains, ex-
isting methods have adopted complementary ap-

(Zhang et al., 2025), optimizing model parame-
ters (Luo et al., 2025), and refining executable ar-
tifacts (Novikov et al., 2025). These routes can
be organized into self-improvement workflows that
propose and evaluate changes using task feedback.
Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-
improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only
task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms
that generate subsequent improvements (Zhang
et al., 2026c; Duan et al., 2026).
Research   on   agent   self-improvement   spans
three increasingly broad scopes of optimization.
Component-level approaches optimize a predefined
part of the system, such as the model or the harness
(execution workflows) (Luo et al., 2025; Zhang
et al., 2026b).   System-level approaches coordi-
nate updates across components, including joint
model–harness optimization and feedback-driven
selection of update targets (Chen et al., 2026d,b;
Hebbar et al., 2026). Meta-level approaches make
1 arXiv:2610.21791v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

improvement procedures editable through operator
scheduling, program modification, and recursive
skill evolution (Tan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c;
Wang et al., 2026). These developments expand
both what can be modified and how modifications
are organized. However, broader editability alone
does not establish how effectively a workflow ad-
dresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether
the ability to organize that workflow improves with
experience. This motivates a central question:   how
can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows
to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize
these workflows more effectively? 
We formulate this challenge as   dynamic work-
flow adaptation   in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks
and evolving workflow orchestration must be con-
sidered together.   As illustrated in Fig. 1, self-
improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks
that vary with task requirements and the agent’s ca-
pability state. Even within a fixed domain, success-
ful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter
the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestra-
tion. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself
a capability that can improve through experience.
Feedback from workflow execution supports the ac-
cumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge
for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution.
These processes form a feedback loop: task-level
updates reshape improvement requirements, while
workflow experience refines the orchestration capa-
bility that guides subsequent updates.
To address this challenge, we propose   RSIFlow ,
a framework that couples   adaptive workflow orches-
tration   with   meta-agent capability evolution . We
instantiate three self-improvement workflows tar-
geting the   Harness ,   Model , and   Artifacts . A meta-
agent uses execution trajectories and environmental
feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks,
select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate gener-
ation and validation. It then distills orchestration
outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-
component principles to revise its own harness, in-
cluding execution procedures and skill invocation.
This experience-driven self-revision closes a recur-
sive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration
outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that
guides subsequent improvements.
Our main contributions are:
• We formulate   dynamic workflow adaptation 
as a key challenge in RSI, highlighting the
coupling between evolving performance bot-
tlenecks and continual refinement of workflow
orchestration.
• We propose   RSIFlow , which adaptively orga-
nizes self-improvement workflows and uses
their observed outcomes to evolve the meta-
agent’s own harness, including its execution
procedures and reusable skills.
• We evaluate   RSIFlow   across six benchmarks
and two backbones, outperforming the strongest
evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark–
backbone settings. Ablations support the bene-
fits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and
meta-harness evolution. 
2   Related Work 
Component-Specific Self-Improvement.   Many
approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a
single predefined component.   STaR (Zelikman
et al., 2022) improves model parameters by re-
peatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales
that yield correct answers. AFlow (Zhang et al.,
2025) searches code-represented workflows, while
Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (Lee et al.,
2026) refines prompt-level harness specifications
using pairwise feedback over revision histories.
Related approaches include DSPy (Khattab et al.,
2024) for language-model pipeline optimization,
GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) for reflective prompt
evolution, and ADAS (Hu et al., 2025) for meta-
agent-guided search over agent programs. In con-
trast, AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) evolves
candidate programs through execution-based evalu-
ation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s
improvement procedure.   Self-Refine (Madaan
et al., 2023) iteratively revises outputs using self-
feedback, while Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023)
retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent at-
tempts and Voyager (Wang et al., 2024) accumu-
lates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness (Chen
et al., 2026d) and HarnessForge (Chen et al.,
2026b) connect external structure and internal ca-
pability by alternating harness refinement with
model optimization. Their coupled updates address
model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed
update order leaves open how to adapt workflow
orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks. 
Adaptive   and   Recursive   Self-Improvement. 
Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA (Hebbar et al.,
2026) uses trajectory and performance feedback to
choose between harness and weight updates, while
its selection policy relies on a frozen language-

3   Methodology 
Fig. 2 provides an overview of RSIFlow. Sec. 3.1
formalizes the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent sys-
tem and the recursive self-improvement process.
Sec. 3.2 describes how the Meta-Agent adap-
tively orchestrates component-specific improve-
ment workflows. Finally, Sec. 3.3 presents how
the Meta-Agent evolves through multi-level skill
formation and Meta-Harness refinement.

Recursive self-improvement workflow.   At evo-
lution round   t , the Meta-Agent   M t   orchestrates and
evaluates candidate updates to the Task-Agent   T t ,
yielding the next-round Task-Agent   T t +1   and work-
flow experience   e t . It distills component-specific
skills and general principles from this experience,
integrating them into its Meta-Harness to form 
M t +1 . The updated knowledge guides diagnosis,
workflow selection, and candidate generation in
subsequent rounds as the Task-Agent’s bottlenecks
evolve. Together,   ( T t +1 , M t +1 )   enter the next evo-
lution round, allowing accumulated workflow ex-
perience to continuously refine the orchestration
mechanism. Details are provided in App. B.1. 
3.3   Meta-agent Capability Evolution
Difference extraction and skill formation.   The
Meta-Agent aligns parent and candidate trajecto-
ries for the same task through shared subgoals, tool
events, or error feedback. These paired compar-
isons connect candidate modifications to local be-
havioral changes and task-level outcomes. From
these comparisons and workflow experience   e t , the
Meta-Agent distills two complementary forms of
reusable knowledge: component-specific skills   S t

eral principles   P t   for cross-component diagnosis
and workflow selection. Each skill or principle is

4   Experiments 
4.1   Experimental Setup
Benchmarks.   We train   RSIFlow   on training data
from three task domains and evaluate it on six pub-
lic benchmarks spanning the same domains:   (1)
code generation,   HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (Liu
et al., 2023).   (2) tool use,   BFCL-v3 (Patil et al.,
2025) and ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025).   (3)
search-QA,   HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and
2Wiki (Ho et al., 2020). Detailed descriptions and
evaluation metrics are in App. A.2 
Baselines.   We compare RSIFlow with three se-
ries of baselines:   (1) model-only evolution , includ-
ing SFT (Ouyang et al., 2022) and GRPO (Shao
et al., 2024);   (2) harness-only evolution , includ-
ing AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025) and Mermaid-
Flow (Zheng et al., 2025);   (3) model-harness both
evolution,   including HarnessForge (Chen et al.,
2026b) and SIA (Hebbar et al., 2026), Hypera-
gent (Zhang et al., 2026c) further evolves the har-
ness of the meta agent, incorporating the evolution
of the meta into the cycle. Detailed configurations
of baselines are provided in App. A.4 
Implementation Details.   We initialize the Task-
Agent of RSIF LOW   with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-
8B (Yang et al., 2025) as the backbone, respec-
tively. The Meta-Agent uses GPT-5.6 Sol as its
base model. We run   R   = 5   evolution rounds and
report the main results with a maximum of two
attempts per evolution round. Additional imple-
mentation details are provided in App. B 
4.2   Main Results 
Tab. 1 compares RSIF LOW   against model-only,
harness-only, and joint model–harness baselines
on six agentic benchmarks and two backbone
sizes, averaging +3.11% over the strongest per-
metric baselines.   RSIF LOW   leads in 11 of 12
benchmark–backbone settings across code gener-
ation, tool use, and search-QA. Its overall scores
reach 51.21% with Qwen3-4B and 59.86% with
Qwen3-8B, surpassing the strongest baseline by
6.06% and 3.86%, respectively. The largest gain oc-
curs on HumanEval+, where RSIF LOW   improves
pass@1 by 14.02% with Qwen3-4B. On MBPP+,
pass@1 improves by an average of 3.91% across
backbones. For tool use, RSIF LOW   achieves the
highest BFCL-v3 scores with both backbones and
the best ACEBench result with Qwen3-4B. On

4.3   Ablation Study 
Table 2 evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration
and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Com-
pared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool
Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20%
, respectively, increasing the three-domain aver-
age by 13.72 %.   While fixed-component work-
flows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive
orchestration achieves the highest scores across all
three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow
by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow
exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by
6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces
average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the
importance of distilling historical feedback into
reusable skills and principles. These results demon-
strate that adaptive component orchestration en-
ables balanced cross-domain improvements, while
experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further
strengthens workflow effectiveness.

4.5   Case Study 
Fig. 5 illustrates five rounds (R1–R5) of RSIFlow
evolution, following a Harness–Harness–Model–
Model–Artifacts sequence. In R1, the Meta-Agent
addresses output-format violations with an output-
contract check (H1), reaching 32.23%. R2 builds
on H1 to introduce receipt-grounded verification
(H2) for unsupported completions, raising the score
to 38.04%. To address persistent semantic errors,
R3 shifts to Model optimization with 3,798 replay
calls for LoRA fine-tuning, reaching 45.46% and
distilling the model-specific skill M1. R4 reuses
and supplements M1 with new evidence, expand-
ing training to 5,397 calls and improving the score
to 47.11%. In R5, execution feedback and accumu-
lated repair guidance support code revision and re-
submission within budget, reaching 51.21% while
preserving the Model and Harness. Across these
rounds, skills and general principles progressively
refine the Meta-Agent’s bottleneck diagnosis and
subsequent workflow orchestration. This lineage
demonstrates how adaptive workflow orchestration
and Meta-Harness evolution reinforce each other,
yielding an overall improvement of 18.98%. 
5   Conclusion 
We   presented   RSIFlow ,   a   recursive   self-
improvement   framework   coupling   adaptive
workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution.
Using   accumulated   execution   feedback,   the
Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and
selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows.
It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes
into reusable skills and principles to evolve its
Meta-Harness.   Across six benchmarks and two
backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest
evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations
validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses
show a favorable performance–budget trade-off.
These results demonstrate that continual Meta-
Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness
alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.
8

Limitations 
RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B
and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This set-
ting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained
agent deployments, where adaptive workflow or-
chestration enables targeted modifications to identi-
fied bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evo-
lution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and
orchestration capabilities. However, whether these
benefits remain significant with larger backbone
models and at cluster scale remains unexplored.
Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-
scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.
RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-
Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable
skills and general principles to improve workflow
orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s
model parameters.   However, this process intro-
duces additional computational overhead, while
adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compro-
mise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of
experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains
to be fully investigated. Future work will explore
counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent de-
ficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and
investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to
improve evolution efficiency and stability.
